Summary (auto): initial discovery focused on air-gapped on-prem deployment for sensitive workloads, discuss updates, key mgmt, hardware constraints, and pilot next steps.

[00:00] Avery Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Avery, account exec for Redwood Inference. With me is Priya, our SE, and Jonah from solutions. How are you all?
[00:08] Martin Kline: Hi, Martin here. Thanks. We're a bit pressed for time so we'll try to be concise.
[00:12] Elena Alvarez: Elena, security. We'll jump into the hard questions quickly.
[00:16] Priya Nair: Great, thanks. Do you want me to kick off with a quick overview of how our on-prem/private works or start with your constraints?
[00:24] Martin: Start with constraints. We're a defence contractor - no internet egress from the segmentation zones where models will run. Air-gapped, FIPS requirements on crypto, and all updates have to go through an offline change control process.
[00:36] Priya: Understood. That's a pretty common pattern for regulated customers. On our side we support an air-gapped package flow: you can import artifacts via signed bundles on USB or secure transfer node, and the control plane can run either as a private control plane in your VPC or completely disconnected; we call that the offline appliance mode.
[00:51] Rakesh Menon: When you say signed bundles, what's the signing model? Do you integrate with our HSM or do you ship a key?
[00:57] Priya: We integrate with customer-managed keys. There are two patterns: 1) you bring your KMS/HSM and we support key wrapping so the bundle is encrypted and signed with a key under your control; 2) for strict air-gap, we provide an offline signing workflow where Redwood signs artifacts and you validate signatures against a provided public key, but many customers prefer to host the signing within their HSM. We can do either.
[01:20] Elena: We have an on-prem HSM (Thales) with FIPS 140-2. We'll need FIPS validated crypto and an audit trail that shows key usage.
[01:28] Priya: We support HSM integrations and can generate audit events for bundle creation/verification. We also have examples for Thales and PKCS#11 integration. We'll share the integration guide.
[01:37] Jonah Park: On the runtime side, our inference runtime can run on bare metal with GPUs. We support multiple quantization profiles which helps when you have limited memory or want to run on lower-spec cards.
[01:49] Martin: Speaking of GPUs, we have strict procurement windows and approved SKUs - Ampere A100 is on the allowed list but there's a 3-month lead time. We also have some older V100 racks. Can Redwood run on V100/older hardware?
[02:03] Priya: Yes - we support multiple hardware backends. Performance will vary; V100 may need different kernel selections and we'll likely recommend more aggressive quantization to fit models within memory. It's doable. For high-throughput low-latency workloads we'd generally recommend A100 or equivalent.
[02:18] Martin: What about NVLink and multi-GPU sharding? We have some racks without NVLink and it's important for our inference patterns.
[02:25] Jonah: We support both single-GPU and multi-GPU sharding. NVLink improves throughput for very large context KV cache workloads; without NVLink we fall back to model-parallel strategies that are more expensive latency-wise. We'll include guidance in the hardware playbook.
[02:40] Rakesh: For offline updates how do you handle security patches for OS and the inference runtime? Our change control requires signed OS images and a maintenance window.
[02:49] Priya: We provide hardened OS images as part of the appliance, and we can package OS patches into the same signed bundle flow. For the runtime we provide versioned artifacts with checksums and signatures. Customers typically test the bundle in a staging air-gapped segment, then promote to production. The patching cadence and who signs is up to you; we can mirror your change control process.
[03:07] Elena: We also need to capture forensic logs - who called what model, at which timestamp, token counts, etc. Does Redwood keep local audit logs that can be exported to our SIEM?
[03:17] Priya: Yes. Audit logs are local, we can retain them on-prem and forward to your log collector (Splunk, ELK) over an internal network. For strictly isolated zones we ship export utilities that create signed log bundles for offline ingestion.
[03:30] Martin: Any concerns about model weights leaving the network? We can't allow model artifacts to be exfiltrated.
[03:35] Avery Chen: Absolutely. In air-gapped mode, model weights and artifacts are stored on local disks only and we can enforce policies so that no outbound network connections are attempted. The offline bundle process ensures artifacts are only introduced via approved physical transfer.
[03:50] Rakesh: What about licensing for open models vs proprietary? We need to track model provenance for audits.
[03:56] Priya: We track model provenance metadata with each bundle: model name, version, quantization profile, and a hash. That metadata is signed and included in the bundle manifest for auditability.
[04:08] Martin: OK. Walk me through a typical pilot - what do we give you, what do you run, and what's the timeline?
[04:14] Priya: Typical pilot for air-gapped starts with a small cluster (2-4 GPUs) on your side or a host you provide. We bring a pilot artifact bundle with a validated model (or you provide a model), a lightweight control plane image for offline install, and a test plan: latency p95, throughput, and functional QA against owned prompts. Timeline is usually 4-6 weeks including procurement and access.
[04:33] Sophia Trent: Procurement is the sticky bit for us. Realistically, we can get 2 A100s in 3 months or use our V100s now for an initial alpha.
[04:41] Jonah: That's fine for a staged approach - alpha on V100s to validate correctness and flows, then perf run on A100s once procured. We'll adjust quantization and batch configs per hardware.
[04:52] Elena: Do you support automatic degradations if a GPU is down? We need reliability and graceful degradation.
[04:58] Priya: The offline appliance supports local failover patterns; we can configure fallback to smaller model variants and queueing policies. However in fully air-gapped clusters you won't have the cloud fallbacks - so we'll design redundancy into the cluster.
[05:12] Martin: About model updates - is there a signed artifact format we can inspect? We need to vet the code in the runtime and the model.
[05:19] Priya: Yes, we publish an artifact spec in the playbook. The bundle contains runtime binaries, model weights (optionally encrypted), manifest.json (signed), and an install script. You can run the installer in a staging environment and verify signatures with your HSM.
[05:33] Rakesh: Are there any components that phone home for telemetry? Our policy forbids outbound telemetry from the classified zones.
[05:41] Avery: In air-gapped/offline mode we can disable all telemetry. telemetry is optional and controlled by config. For enterprise contracts we support an opt-in for limited telemetry but in your case we'd disable it entirely and provide local logs.
[05:54] Elena: For compliance we'll need SOC 2 or equivalent proof from Redwood and also FIPS certs where applicable. Do you have SOC2?
[06:01] Avery: Yes, we are SOC 2 Type II. We also maintain documentation around encryption practices and FIPS-compatible configurations. I'll send the SOC2 SOC report redacted and the relevant architecture playbook.
[06:12] Martin: Will you provide a threat model for the appliance? We'll need that to satisfy our internal cert board.
[06:18] Priya: Yes, we can provide an appliance threat model and a secure deployment guide that maps to typical certification checklists.
[06:24] Rakesh: What about offline licensing updates - e.g., enabling new model variants after purchase. Can that be done via the same signed bundle process?
[06:31] Priya: Exactly - feature flags and model entitlements can be pushed via signed bundles. The control plane enforces entitlements based on the signed manifest.
[06:40] Martin: OK. A few technical clarifications: does the runtime require kernel modules or special drivers that are tricky to get approved? We try to minimize surface area for the cert board.
[06:50] Jonah: We use standard NVIDIA drivers; no weird kernel modules beyond what the vendor drivers require. For some performance kernels we include optimized CUDA libraries, but those are user-space. We'll document any kernel-level requirements.
[07:03] Rakesh: Power/cooling constraints: we have max rack power per unit. Can you provide expected power draw for A100 vs V100 configurations?
[07:11] Priya: We'll provide a hardware sizing sheet with power, thermal, and rack U requirements per GPU and typical NVLink configs.
[07:18] Elena: For encryption at rest, do you support LUKS with HSM-backed keys?
[07:23] Priya: Yes - disk-level encryption can be integrated with your KMS/HSM and we support LUKS or vendor-specific encryption.
[07:30] Martin: Are there known limitations with larger models and quantization in air-gapped mode? Any runtime features disabled offline?
[07:38] Jonah: Feature parity is near-complete. The only limitations are cloud-managed autoscaling and some caching features that rely on a distributed control plane. Locally we do prefix caching and KV cache management; it's all supported but implemented differently for isolated clusters.
[07:54] Martin: Good. Let's cover pricing high-level. Is pricing license-based for private or usage?
[07:59] Avery: For private deployments we typically do a platform fee (annual) plus support and optional reserved capacity for Dedicated. For on-prem air-gapped customers we do an enterprise license + support + optional professional services for integration. We'll follow up with a draft commercial term sheet.
[08:13] Sophia: Procurement will want numbers for an initial 2 GPU pilot and a 6 GPU prod cluster.
[08:18] Avery: We'll include price options in the SOW.
[08:21] Martin: One more thing: can you provide a sample offline update runbook - step-by-step so our ops can validate change control?
[08:27] Priya: Yes, we'll include a sample runbook showing bundle creation, signature verification with PKCS#11 examples, staging validation, and production promotion steps.
[08:38] Rakesh: For testing, we want reproducible benchmarks: p95 latency, throughput at batch sizes, and token cost. Will Redwood run benchmarks in our environment?
[08:46] Jonah: We can run benchmarking with your test harness inside the air-gapped environment. Typically we bring a benchmark artifact and a harness that you run; we analyze results together.
[08:56] Elena: Are there export control considerations for model weights? We're in defence; some models might be restricted.
[09:02] Avery: We'll work with your legal and export compliance teams to ensure any model distribution aligns with export control. We also support customers bringing their own models so there is no distribution risk from Redwood.
[09:12] Martin: That covers the main items. Next steps recap?
[09:15] Avery: Recap - we'll send SOC2 and the security playbook, Priya will draft pilot SOW and sample runbook, and we'll schedule an SE-led deep dive after you confirm hardware SKUs.
[09:26] Martin: Sounds good. We'll aim to get the SKU list by Friday.
[09:30] Elena: Also copy our procurement and compliance contacts on the follow-up.
[09:34] Avery: Will do. Thanks everyone.
[09:36] Martin: Thanks.

End of call.
